findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
findings.body: The goroutine derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the API handler returns its successful unified-storage response, Kubernetes/Grafana can cancel that request context, which immediately cancels the legacy Create call (and the same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection). Consequently, many or all best-effort legacy writes can be aborted before they run, especially under normal request teardown. Derive the async context from a cancellation-detached context (while preserving required values) and apply the 10-second timeout to that context.

findings.title: Independent async goroutines can apply legacy mutations out of order
findings.body: Each successful unified write launches an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or ordering. For example, a create followed immediately by an update or delete can execute in legacy as update/delete before create, or create after delete, leaving legacy with a stale or incorrect object even though unified storage is correct. Since mode 3 is intended to retain legacy as a safe copy, writes need an ordered queue/worker mechanism (at least per resource) rather than unconstrained concurrent goroutines.

findings.title: Legacy update recomputes the update instead of mirroring the unified result
findings.body: The legacy async call receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has completed. UpdatedObjectInfo is evaluated against the store's current/old object, so evaluating it again against potentially stale legacy state can generate a different payload, apply a stale resource version, or fail differently. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated the update and wrapped the unified result before passing it to legacy, ensuring both stores received the same object. Preserve that behavior by passing a wrapper containing the successful unified result to the legacy write.

findings.title: Legacy outages can create an unbounded number of blocked goroutines
findings.body: Every successful write creates a new goroutine that may remain blocked for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). There is no queue capacity, worker limit, or backpressure. During a legacy outage and sustained write traffic this grows goroutine count and outstanding requests proportionally to traffic, risking memory exhaustion and scheduler degradation in the API server. Use bounded workers/queueing and define an overflow policy.

findings.title: Delete metric uses resource name as the kind label
findings.body: The successful delete metric passes `name` where all other calls pass `options.Kind`. Object names are effectively unbounded and often user-controlled, so each deleted object creates a distinct Prometheus label value/time series that is never reclaimed by the metric vector. This can cause unbounded metric memory/cardinality growth. Pass `options.Kind` instead.

findings.title: Unified-storage failures are recorded as legacy durations
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration using the unified-storage timing even though no legacy write was attempted. The same error exists in Update at line 129, and DeleteCollection records the async legacy duration as storage duration at line 166. This makes backend/error metrics and alerts report the wrong failing system; use recordStorageDuration for unified operations and recordLegacyDuration for the async legacy operation.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests do not actually verify asynchronous legacy mirroring
findings.body: Both the legacy and unified mock wrappers share one mock and use the same method names and argument matchers. For example, the legacy Create expectation at line 31 also matches the unified Storage.Create invocation, so the tests cannot identify which backend was called; the storage-failure case similarly configures only a purported legacy expectation. The tests also neither wait for the goroutine nor assert mock expectations. As a result, they pass without proving that legacy writes happen asynchronously, are skipped after unified failure, or receive the expected payload. Use separate mocks (or backend-identifying expectations), synchronize completion, and assert expectations.
